title: Observing and Controlling Features in Vision-Language-Action Models
action_head: mixed: discrete action tokens (OpenVLA, pi0-FAST) and flow/diffusion action expert (pi0, pi0.5); closed-loop steering only on pi0.5
methods: linear observers (probes) on mean-pooled transformer representations per layer
additive steering along observer directions (alpha sweep)
minimal-norm closed-form controller that projects observer predictions into a target interval, broadcast to all tokens
baselines: prompting, value-vector steering (Haon et al.), rejection sampling, action clipping
question: Are robot state and action features linearly observable in VLA representations, and can a minimal linear intervention on those representations steer closed-loop behavior to satisfy user constraints without hurting task success?
key_findings: All model-dataset pairs (LIBERO, DROID, BridgeData V2) contain linearly decodable state and action information: Cartesian state R2 0.81-1.00, orientation 0.53-0.99, action probes 'well below'; gripper state near-perfect, gripper command more variable (Fig. 3).
Action decodability drops by roughly a third from LIBERO to real DROID while state decodability is unchanged; the sim-real gap is larger than the gap between architectures.

Pushing along observer directions gives graded, ordered changes in continuous actions in both pi0 (flow) and pi0-FAST (tokens) across 50 LIBERO episodes; gripper response is less regular; later layers are less sensitive.

Transport-lift constraints (LIBERO-Spatial, 100 rollouts per method): the controller raises constraint satisfaction while keeping task success; rejection sampling stays below 10% satisfaction even at K=100 (with +583% inference time); value vectors ~74% for the upper bound and 0% for the lower bound; action clipping also works (Fig. 6).

Grasp preference: wine bottle base grasp 28% base policy, 40% best prompt, 3% value vectors, 73% controller (100 initial conditions); real mug handle grasp 14% / 46% / 38% / 74% (50 rollouts) (Table I).
Real-robot safe-object choice: banana over fork 52% base, 40% prompt, 64% value vectors, 100% controller; glass over plastic bowl 48% / 62% / 94% / 100% (50 rollouts each) (Table II).

benchmarks: DROID dataset and DROID Franka hardware
evidence.scale: probing: held-out 10% split; output sensitivity: 50 LIBERO episodes; closed-loop: 100 rollouts per method per sim experiment (10 tasks x 10 for lift), 50 rollouts per method per hardware task
evidence.statistics: partial: std across tasks for the lift experiment; otherwise percentages without CIs or tests
evidence.baselines: unmodified policy, prompting, value-vector steering (Haon et al. 2509.00328), rejection sampling, action clipping

causal_validation: Yes: interventions along observer directions change generated actions in a graded way, and the closed-form controller changes executed behavior (grasp choice, object choice, lift) in closed loop.
closed_loop: Yes: LIBERO simulation and real DROID hardware with pi0.5.
limitations_stated: Observers need labeled data, which may be unavailable at scale.
Interventions target the transformer/VLM part, not the flow-matching head.
No safety guarantees or bounds on intervention effects; complementary to output-level filters.
critique: Placed in the SAE section, but no dictionary learning is used: this is supervised probe-and-steer. It is the probe-based counterpart to 2603.19183 (same group), with stronger closed-loop baselines.

Categorical observers (grasp modality, object choice) are fit on the 50 base-policy rollouts of the same scene and task, so each controller is task-specific; '100% safe object' shows controllability in a fixed scene, not a general safety feature.

The strongest result is the comparison against prompting and value vectors on hardware; prompting failing to change grasp modality matches the language-insensitivity findings in 2603.19233 and 2610.06235.

This paper reports graded steering along observer directions, while 2608.13474 found a progress probe direction non-steerable. The difference likely lies in what is probed (action-adjacent quantities like lift and grasp here vs a visual progress cue at layer 0 there), which is consistent with the belief-vs-action distinction in 2610.20840.
No CIs on 50-rollout percentages; differences such as 64% vs 100% are large, but 46% vs 74% has substantial uncertainty at n=50.
one_line: Linear probes read robot state and action from four VLAs, and a closed-form linear intervention that keeps the probe's prediction inside a target range steers pi0.5's grasp and object choices on a real robot far better than prompting or value-vector steering, at ~1% compute overhead.
